# Labour Party Manifesto 2005 Summary

## Overview and Vision

The 2005 Labour Manifesto, titled "Britain Forward, Not Back," presents New Labour's plan for a third term, built on the principle that government must provide opportunity and security for all in a changing world. The foreword, written as a personal message from the party leader, reflects on achievements since 1997—economic stability, improved public services, and reduced poverty—while acknowledging difficult decisions made, including on Iraq.

## Economic Record and Plans

Labour claims unprecedented economic success: the longest period of uninterrupted growth in modern history, lowest sustained interest rates for a generation, and two million more people in work since 1997. The manifesto commits to maintaining economic stability through continued Bank of England independence, keeping inflation at two percent, and borrowing only to invest.

Key economic pledges include not raising basic or top income tax rates, raising the minimum wage to £5.35 by October 2006, and aiming for an 80 percent employment rate. The party promises to reform Incapacity Benefit and continue welfare-to-work programmes while supporting enterprise through reduced regulation and investment in science and innovation.

## Education

Education remains "number one priority." The manifesto celebrates improved primary school results, with ten-year-olds ranked third globally in literacy. Plans include making every secondary school an independent specialist school, expanding the Academies programme to 200 schools by 2010, and introducing specialised vocational diplomas for 14-19 year-olds.

Investment in education will continue rising as a share of national income. The manifesto commits to 50 percent of young people attending higher education by 2010 and caps tuition fees at £3,000 (inflation-adjusted) for the entire Parliament.

## Healthcare

NHS spending has doubled since 1997 and will triple by 2008. The manifesto celebrates 27,000 additional doctors and 79,000 more nurses, with waiting times dramatically reduced. Future commitments include eliminating waits over 18 weeks from referral to treatment by 2008, offering patients free choice of hospital, and tackling MRSA through improved hygiene standards.

Public health initiatives include banning high-fat foods from school meals, restricting advertising of unhealthy foods to children, and implementing smokefree legislation in enclosed public places and workplaces, with exemptions for some pubs and membership clubs.

## Crime and Security

The manifesto claims crime has fallen 30 percent since 1997. Key pledges include a neighbourhood policing team for every community, expanding Community Support Officers to 24,000, and introducing compulsory drug testing for property and drug offenders. Anti-social behaviour measures will be strengthened, and ID cards with biometric data will be introduced voluntarily as people renew passports.

On immigration, a points-based system will be established prioritizing skilled workers, with fingerprinting for visa applicants and electronic border tracking within five years.

## Families and Welfare

The manifesto commits to ending child poverty, starting by halving it by 2010-11. Paid maternity leave will increase to nine months by 2007, aiming for twelve months by Parliament's end. Universal childcare will be established with 3,500 Sure Start Children's Centres by 2010, and homeownership will increase by another one to two million.

## International Policy

Labour pledges continued EU leadership, putting the Constitutional Treaty to referendum. On defence, the party commits to maintaining the independent nuclear deterrent while modernizing armed forces. The manifesto acknowledges Iraq War controversies while calling for unity in supporting Iraqi democracy.

Climate change and African poverty are highlighted as G8 presidency priorities, with commitment to reaching 0.7 percent of national income for development aid by 2013.

## Constitutional Reform

Promises include completing House of Lords reform, devolving more power to local authorities, and enhancing Welsh Assembly powers. The manifesto defends the Human Rights Act while promising to address "abusive or frivolous claims" and establish a Commission on Equality and Human Rights.

# Summary of the Green Party Manifesto 2005

The Green Party's 2005 manifesto, titled "The Real Choice for Real Change," presents a comprehensive vision for building a sustainable society based on social, economic, and environmental justice. The document outlines policies across ten key areas.

## Economics
The party advocates for wealth redistribution through progressive taxation, including 50% tax on earnings over £50,000 and 60% over £100,000. They propose replacing VAT with eco-taxes, introducing Land Value Tax, and promoting economic localisation through community banks and local currencies. The Greens oppose UK entry into the euro and support workers' rights, including the right to unionise.

## Energy and Climate Change
Central to their environmental policy is adopting the "Contraction and Convergence" framework, targeting 20% carbon dioxide reduction by 2010 and 85% by 2030. They propose introducing a carbon tax, increasing renewable energy to 40% by 2020, and closing nuclear power stations. A Cabinet-level post for climate change would be created.

## Welfare
The manifesto introduces the Citizen's Income—an unconditional payment to all UK residents covering basic needs—and a Citizen's Pension linked to average earnings. These universal benefits aim to replace means-testing and empower individuals while reducing inequality.

## Health and Education
The party commits to restoring NHS founding principles, opposing privatisation, abolishing prescription charges, and increasing health funding to EU average levels. In education, they would scrap tuition fees, restore maintenance grants, abolish SATs, and introduce individualised learning plans.

## Transport
Priorities include reducing car dependency through improved public transport, returning rail networks to public ownership, implementing road pricing that reflects true motoring costs, and tackling aviation growth through fuel taxation.

## Environment
A Zero Waste Strategy would target 60% domestic recycling by 2010. The party supports protecting biodiversity, opposing genetic modification, ending animal testing, and adopting the precautionary principle for new technologies.

## Food and Farming
The Greens propose an Organics Target Bill for 30% organic production by 2012, replacing the Common Agricultural Policy, banning GM food, and tackling supermarket monopolies.

## Crime and Justice
The approach emphasises community-based crime prevention, increased community policing, tougher gun control, restorative justice programmes, and protecting human rights while opposing national ID cards.

## Democracy
Constitutional reforms include proportional representation for Westminster and local elections, an elected House of Lords, devolved regional government, and a written constitution. The party opposes the proposed EU constitution while supporting EU reform.

## International Policy
The manifesto advocates for an ethical foreign policy, nuclear disarmament, reducing military spending to EU average, cancelling debt for the 52 poorest countries, increasing aid to 1% of GNI, and replacing WTO rules with a General Agreement on Sustainable Trade. The party opposes the Iraq war and supports humane asylum policies.
